title: Installing MySQL and Connecting
summary: Install MySQL 8.4 or 9 on Windows, macOS or Linux, or run it in Docker, then connect with the mysql client, run your first commands and fix the three classic connection errors.
introduction: Before you can create a table you need a running server and a client to talk to it. This lesson compares the installation routes for each operating system, shows the fastest way to get a disposable server with Docker, and then connects with the mysql command-line client that every later lesson uses. You will also meet the connection mistakes that stop most beginners on day one: the wrong host, the wrong port, and the root account that refuses a perfectly good password.
learningObjectives: Install MySQL Community Server with the package or container that fits your system
Connect to a server with the mysql client, choosing host, port, user and database
Run the first diagnostic commands and quit cleanly

blocks.text: MySQL Community Server is free. Which download you pick depends on your operating system and on whether you want a permanent installation or a throwaway server for learning. All routes give you the same server and the same `mysql` client.

rows: The MSI launches *MySQL Configurator*, which sets the root password, picks the port and registers a Windows service
`brew install mysql@8.4` or the DMG package
Homebrew's plain `mysql` formula installs the latest 9.x innovation release instead
Ubuntu's own `mysql-server` package is still the 8.0 series; add Oracle's repository first to get 8.4 or 9.x
Nothing to uninstall later; data lives in the container or in a volume you attach

blocks.text: If Docker is installed, one command downloads the image, initialises a data directory, sets the root password and starts the server. `-p 3306:3306` publishes the server's port on your machine so desktop tools can reach it; `-d` runs it in the background. `docker run` prints the new container's id and returns while the server spends a few seconds initialising. `docker exec -it` then runs the client *inside* the container, which avoids every networking question for now.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.code:
docker run --name mysql-dev \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=change-me \
  -p 3306:3306 \
  -d mysql:8.4

docker exec -it mysql-dev mysql -u root -p

blocks.text: The connection id, patch version and copyright year in the banner depend on your build. The `mysql>` prompt means the server accepted the password and is waiting for SQL.

On Ubuntu and Debian the server starts as a system service as soon as the package is installed. `mysql_secure_installation` is an interactive script that sets a password policy, removes anonymous accounts and the `test` database and disables remote root login; answer yes to all of it even on a development machine, because it costs nothing and matches production.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install mysql-server
sudo systemctl status mysql
sudo mysql_secure_installation

blocks.content:
● mysql.service - MySQL Community Server
     Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/mysql.service; enabled; preset: enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Sat 2026-11-14 09:12:03 UTC; 2min 10s ago

blocks.text: The `systemctl status` lines above are the ones that matter: `enabled` means the service starts at boot and `active (running)` means it is listening now. Timestamps will be your own.

`mysql` is a small terminal program that sends what you type to a server and prints the answer. It takes the connection details as options; a database name as the last argument selects it immediately, which saves a `USE` statement.

rows: Prompt for the password; never type it on the command line, where it would land in your shell history
Host. `localhost` uses the Unix socket on Linux and macOS; `127.0.0.1` forces a TCP connection

blocks.text: Two functions confirm who you are and what you are talking to. `USER()` reports the account and the host the server sees you connecting from, which becomes important in the [users lesson](/tutorials/mysql/users-privileges). Every statement ends with a semicolon; the client waits patiently on a new line until you type one.
Server settings are *system variables*, and `SHOW VARIABLES` reads them. The `LIKE` pattern narrows the list, because a server has several hundred.

items: `\s` (or `STATUS`) prints the connection details: user, server version, character set, uptime.
`\G` instead of `;` prints each row vertically, which is the only readable way to look at wide rows.
`\c` throws away a half-typed statement when you have lost track of quotes or brackets.
`\q` or `exit` closes the connection and returns to the shell.
`help` lists every client command; `help contents` opens the server-side SQL help.

blocks.text: Three connection errors and their fixes

items: `ERROR 2002 (HY000): Can't connect to local MySQL server through socket` means no server is listening on the socket file. Either the service is not running (`sudo systemctl start mysql`) or it only listens on TCP, so add `-h 127.0.0.1`.
`ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost' (using password: YES)` means the password is wrong, or the account exists for a different host than the one you are connecting from.

`ERROR 1698 (28000): Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'` on Debian and Ubuntu packages means root authenticates through the `auth_socket` plugin: only the system root user may log in, without a password. Run `sudo mysql`, then create a normal account for yourself as shown in [Users and Privileges](/tutorials/mysql/users-privileges).

blocks.title: A container's localhost is not your localhost
blocks.text: When you connect from your desktop to the port published by Docker, the server sees the connection arriving from the Docker bridge network, not from `localhost`. An account created as `'app'@'localhost'` is therefore rejected with error 1045 even though the password is right. Create accounts for containers as `'app'@'%'` (any host), or run the client inside the container with `docker exec`, as above.

The command line is enough for this tutorial, but you will also meet *MySQL Workbench*, Oracle's desktop client with a visual schema designer, and *MySQL Shell* (`mysqlsh`), a newer command-line client with SQL, JavaScript and Python modes that provides the parallel dump and load utilities used in [Backup and Restore](/tutorials/mysql/backup-restore). Editors such as VS Code and DBeaver connect too. All of them ask for the same four things: host, port, user and password.

blocks.title: Keep a scratch server
blocks.text: A Docker container you can delete with `docker rm -f mysql-dev` is the ideal place to try every destructive statement in this tutorial. Recreate it in ten seconds and nothing you broke matters.

questions.question: Which option sets the port when connecting with the mysql client?
questions.explanation: `-P` (capital) is the port; lower-case `-p` asks for the password. Mixing them up is a classic first-day mistake.

questions.question: On Ubuntu, `ERROR 1698 (28000): Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'` usually means you typed the wrong password.
questions.explanation: Error 1698 comes from the auth_socket plugin: the packaged root account only accepts the system root user. Use `sudo mysql` and create your own account.
